Better High-Yield Dividend Stock: AT&T vs. General Mills ©@9comeback from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

AT&T yields 5.2% and General Mills yields 7.0%, and both companies plan to hold their dividends flat for now.

AT&T's dividend used 44% of its free cash flow over the last twelve months, while General Mills' used 85%.

AT&T expects free cash flow of $21 billion or more by 2028, while General Mills guides for lower operating profit this fiscal year as it pays down debt.

SpaceX's push into wireless is the main new risk to AT&T's cash flow, and General Mills' debt sits above its own target.

General Mills (GIS:NYSE) declared another $0.61 quarterly dividend on Sept. 29. That's the same rate as before, a 7.0% yield.

AT&T (T:NYSE) isn't raising its dividend either. With its third-quarter results on Oct. 21, it said it plans to keep paying $1.11 a share a year, a 5.2% yield.

So with neither dividend growing, which is the better high-yield buy?

6 safe dividend stocks paying retirees 6%+ yields

There are over 100 stocks paying 6%+ annual dividends today.

But after an extensive investment review leveraging TIKR's proprietary data, we now believe only six of them are truly safe for retirees.

They're all yours for free as part of our new investment report, which you can access right here.

AT&T is trading copper for fiber

AT&T's dividend per share fell from $2.08 in fiscal 2020 to $1.11 in fiscal 2025, which explains the negative 5-year rate. What's left is well-covered. It used 44% of free cash flow over the twelve months to Sept. 30, 2026, and 46% on analysts' fiscal 2026 consensus. Since fiscal 2023, the dividend has cost just over $8 billion a year, under half of free cash flow every year:

AT&T (T): free cash flow vs. dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2025 (TIKR)

That cash comes from a business that's moving from copper to fiber. Third-quarter revenue rose 5.3% from a year earlier to $32.3 billion. AT&T had a record 769,000 internet net adds in what it calls Advanced Connectivity, while Legacy revenue fell 24.5%.

On the third-quarter call, CEO John Stankey called "a fiber-fed broadband customer with a great wireless service on top of it" the industry's most durable combination. SpaceX wants to compete for the wireless half of that. AT&T stock fell 8% on Oct. 23 after Bloomberg reported that SpaceX is in talks for access to at least 80,000 US cell sites.

General Mills is paying down debt first

General Mills is also holding its dividend flat, but its reason is debt. CFO Kofi Bruce said on the Sept. 23 first-quarter call, "we remain fully committed to our dividend, and in the near term, we expect to maintain the current rate per share while we prioritize deleverage." He expects it to take "at least a couple of years" to get back to the company's 3x net debt to EBITDA target.

AT&T Lays the First Fiber at Its 54-Acre Plano Campus, Reinforcing Its Long-Term Investment in North Texas

PLANO, Texas, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AT&T (NYSE: T) today broke ground on its new global headquarters in Plano, Texas, marking the start of construction with a distinct AT&T milestone: the installation of the campus's first fiber connection.

The new headquarters represents a strategic investment in AT&T's people, culture, and employee experience. Spanning 54 acres and 2.2 million square feet, the seven-building campus will bring AT&T's Dallas-Fort Worth teams together in an integrated, horizontal headquarters designed to foster collaboration and innovation. With workspaces and amenities shaped around employees' needs, the campus will also help AT&T attract, develop, and retain talent for the future.

Engineered as a workplace of the future, the new headquarters will demonstrate what AT&T connectivity makes possible at scale. AT&T fiber and wireless will provide the speed, capacity and low latency needed for AI, real-time collaboration, and emerging workplace technologies. An approximately 250-foot working cell tower, together with fiber and 5G throughout the campus, will provide advanced connectivity for employees and improve wireless connectivity in the surrounding community. The tower will also serve as a recognizable Plano landmark and symbol of AT&T's commitment to a more connected future.

To celebrate the first fiber connection, AT&T executives and employees were joined by Plano Mayor John Muns; Scott Armstrong, principal at Gensler; Eric Hage, president of KDC; and Andy Leatherman, vice chairman at CBRE.

John Stankey, chairman and CEO of AT&T, spoke about what the campus will mean for the company: "Our new headquarters in Plano is an investment for our current and future employees, and our North Texas community. With this new campus, we're creating the environment that makes life better, drives collaboration and serves our customers for decades to come."

John Muns, mayor of Plano, said, "Today marks an exciting milestone for AT&T and the City of Plano," said Mayor John Muns. "This new global headquarters represents a significant investment in our community and reinforces Plano's reputation as a place where businesses can grow and succeed. We're proud to see this project taking shape and the opportunities it will bring to Plano."

Scott Armstrong, principal at Gensler, said, "Great workplaces do more than support the way people work. They create connections, strengthen culture, and provide a sense of belonging. The vision for AT&T's new headquarters creates a world-class destination where innovative workplaces, exceptional amenities, and thoughtfully designed experiences come together to support people in new ways. It is a forward-looking campus that honors the strength of AT&T's legacy while creating an environment designed to inspire connection, innovation, and the possibilities of what comes next."

The thesis was published on September 12th, when the stock was trading at $25.20, and CMCSA lost less than 1% since then. CMCSA shares declined by 20% a few weeks ago due to concerns about intensifying broadband competition, pressure on subscriber numbers and pricing, and weaker theme park attendance, reinforced by KeyBanc's downgrade. In this article, we will summarize the bulls' thesis on CMCSA. Comcast Corporation's share was trading at $25 right now. Comcast Corporation (NASDAQ:CMCSA) operates across broadband and wireless connectivity, NBCUniversal's media and streaming assets, film and television studios, Sky, and Universal theme parks. That cleaner structure is central to understanding the stock, but it comes as Comcast's core broadband business faces tougher competition from fiber and wireless rivals.

T vs. VZ: Which Telecom Stock is a Better Investment Right Now?
Aritra Chatterjee

The growing demand for high-speed connectivity, 5G services and fiber broadband is creating opportunities for telecommunications companies. As consumers and businesses increasingly depend on reliable, high-capacity networks, telecom operators are investing in infrastructure expansion, network modernization and converged service offerings to strengthen customer relationships and drive recurring revenues. Against this backdrop, AT&T, Inc. T and Verizon Communications Inc. VZ remain two prominent players competing for a larger share of the U.S. telecommunications market.

AT&T is pursuing a fiber-led growth strategy, combining its wireless capabilities with expanding broadband infrastructure to improve customer retention and capture rising connectivity demand. Verizon is strengthening its wireless business, expanding its fiber footprint through the Frontier acquisition and pursuing opportunities in AI infrastructure and enterprise connectivity. Let us examine the growth opportunities and challenges facing AT&T and Verizon to determine which stock offers a more compelling investment proposition.

The Case for T

AT&T is strengthening its position in the telecommunications market through investments in fiber broadband, 5G connectivity and converged services. Its strategy focuses on expanding its advanced connectivity footprint while increasing the number of customers subscribing to multiple services. This approach is supporting recurring revenue growth and creating opportunities to improve customer lifetime value.

The company's fiber expansion remains a key growth driver. In third-quarter 2026, AT&T added 442,000 fiber Internet connections and 327,000 fixed wireless connections. Its fiber footprint reached approximately 39.7 million locations, keeping management on track to exceed 40 million locations by year-end 2026. The company is targeting 60 million fiber locations by 2030. Advanced home Internet service revenues increased 23.4% year over year to $2.98 billion, reflecting growing demand for fiber and AT&T Internet Air services.

AT&T is also benefiting from stronger customer convergence. Its advanced home Internet convergence rate reached 42.8% in the third quarter, while the number of converged relationships increased by approximately 350,000. By combining wireless and broadband services, the company aims to improve customer retention and generate additional revenue from existing relationships.

However, AT&T faces considerable financial and operational challenges. Its aggressive investments in spectrum and fiber have increased balance-sheet pressure. Net debt reached $149.82 billion at the end of the third quarter, compared with $126.4 billion in the preceding quarter, primarily reflecting the EchoStar spectrum purchase. Its net debt-to-adjusted EBITDA ratio increased to 3.13 from 2.68, potentially limiting financial flexibility.

The company faces stiff competition from other major players in the industry such as T-Mobile US, Inc. TMUS, Comcast and Verizon. Stiff competition and market saturation are weighing on margins. Growing competition in the wireless market is affecting customer acquisition economics. Although AT&T's postpaid phone ARPU increased approximately 4% year over year, promotional discounts continued to offset some pricing benefits.

Musk Says SpaceX "Could Just Acquire That Legacy Telco." AT&T and Verizon Own What He Wants ©U.S. Air Force photo and kb group via Canva
Key Takeaways

Elon Musk said SpaceX "could just acquire" a legacy telco to use its spectrum, after Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile reportedly turned down SpaceX's requests to run on their networks.

Musk's comment shows that the spectrum AT&T and Verizon own is the asset SpaceX wants. For shareholders, that matters more than the odds of an actual bid.

A buyer would take on AT&T's debt of about $160 billion and would have to pay for Verizon's $20.1 billion of fiscal 2025 free cash flow. Any deal would also face FCC and antitrust review.

AT&T trades at 8.8x forward earnings, below its five-year average of 9.1x. The next thing to watch is the FCC's review of SpaceX's own spectrum purchase.

SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) wants to be a phone company, and the big carriers aren't helping. Verizon (VZ:NYSE), AT&T (T:NYSE) and T-Mobile have reportedly all turned down Elon Musk's requests to let SpaceX's mobile service run on their networks.

So Musk has floated another way in. A clip of him talking about Starlink and the telcos was played on this week's episode of Moonshots with Peter Diamandis. In it, he said:

"I think SpaceX will be able to get very far with the spectrum that it's acquired. But, you know, at a certain point, if we're able to make much better use of the spectrum than, say, a legacy telco is, we could just acquire that legacy telco and use the spectrum, you know, 10 times more effectively."

Why rent when you can buy?

Dave Blundin, founder of Link Ventures and a regular on the show, went further: "We're going to have Starlink phones, we're going to have Starlink services, and it will decimate terrestrial."

SpaceX keeps buying its way in

SpaceX has been paying up for spectrum. It spent $17 billion on spectrum from EchoStar, a deal the FCC approved in May. On Nov. 10, the FCC accepted SpaceX's filing to buy 800 MHz licenses from Grain Management. The Wall Street Journal reported that deal could cost about $8 billion.

The carriers have pushed back each time. Through CTIA, their trade group, they warned the FCC that a wider spectrum buildout could hurt consumers who count on ever-growing wireless capacity. And Semafor reported that AT&T and T-Mobile would cut Boost Mobile off their spectrum if SpaceX goes ahead with a Boost takeover.

title: What Is The Biggest Threat To Charter Communications Stock?
detail:
What Is The Biggest Threat To Charter Communications Stock?
Trefis Team

Charter Communications (CHTR) stock has lost 35.2% over the past year, while the S&P 500 returned 12.8%. If you hold the shares, the worry is whether something in the business itself is slipping. On its November 6, 2026 call, management admitted that Charter has not generated the customer growth it expects and launched a new operating model to return the company to growth. So what is going wrong in the business Charter depends on most?

Charter Is Losing Internet Customers As Competition Grows

Rivals are targeting Charter's home internet customers, a threat management itself raised. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, Charter's own footprint lost 156,000 internet customers before counting Cox, more than the 109,000 it lost a year earlier. Cox, which Charter acquired in a deal that closed on August 19, 2026, lost another 77,000.

Management named the rivals on the same call: expanded fixed wireless competition, fiber overlap, mobile substitution, and aggressive promotions by certain competitors. It also said its most loyal long-term customers are too often at risk from aggressive price competition. Satellite providers are rivals too. Management has not seen meaningful share loss to Starlink, but it called the low Earth orbit providers very well-capitalized and said it takes them seriously.

How Much Of Charter's Revenue Comes From Internet?

Internet is Charter's largest business, bringing in $23.8 billion in fiscal 2025, 43.4% of the company's revenue. That revenue grew 1.7% in fiscal 2025, after 1.4% in fiscal 2024, so the business was barely growing in either year. Across the whole company, management said pro forma revenue fell 1.5% in the third quarter, driven by lower residential revenue.

Investors already pay far less for Charter's sales as a whole than they used to. At the end of September 2026, Charter traded at 0.233 times sales, the lowest of any quarter end in records going back to the end of 2016, and far below the 2.7 it reached at the end of 2020. Even after a rebound in the past month, the stock closed on November 11, 2026 at 45.1% below its highest close of the past year.

How Worried Should Charter Holders Be?

The threat is real but slow, and the price appears to assume much of it already. Management counts 34 million internet customers across the combined company, and one quarter's losses are small against that base.

The early evidence is encouraging but incomplete. Since Charter launched Spectrum Day in the Cox footprint on September 16, management said internet sales are up significantly there, though it expects those trends to vary after the launch period. Yet management has not said when Charter will return to growth.

AT&T (T) stock trades at 11.6 times earnings, against 21.9 for the median S&P 500 company. Over the past twelve months, the shares lost 6.1%, dividends included, while the S&P 500 gained 12.8%. Either a sound phone and internet business is on sale, or the market has a fair reason to pay less for it. So what does a buyer actually get at that price?

AT&T Buyers Get Strong Margins And Free Cash Flow

A buyer gets a business that turns a large share of its sales into cash. The Communications segment accounts for nearly all of that business, having brought in $121 billion of AT&T's $126 billion revenue in fiscal 2025. Over the twelve months to September 2026, AT&T recorded an operating margin of 21.4%, against 19.0% for the median S&P 500 company.

Cash forms the stronger part of the case. For every $100 of AT&T's market value, the company generated about $11.70 of free cash flow over those twelve months. AT&T also bought back $9.3 billion of its stock, and its dividend yields 5.2%.

The profit behind the low multiple did fall, dropping to $13.1 billion in the twelve months to September 2026 from $22.2 billion a year earlier. Yet operating income, the profit from running the business, rose to $27.6 billion from $24.2 billion. In other words, the business itself earned more even as the bottom line shrank.

What Does AT&T Look Like Over Five Years?

Over five years, AT&T has barely grown: revenue was $129 billion in the twelve months to September 2026, against $128 billion five years earlier.

The pickup is recent: revenue grew 3.5% in the latest twelve months, against a 1.9% average over the three twelve-month periods to September 2026. Management said on its October 21, 2026 call that growth comes from its Advanced Connectivity segment, where service revenue grew 6.1% in the third quarter. The call uses different segments from the fiscal 2025 figures above. Service revenue in the older Legacy segment, which is powering down copper-based services, fell about 25% in the third quarter from a year earlier.

Debt remains the risk an owner takes on. At the end of September, AT&T carried total debt of $178 billion, equaling 117.1% of its market value against 19.5% for the S&P 500. The company's leverage ratio, measuring net debt against adjusted EBITDA, rose to 3.13 times at the end of the third quarter from 2.68 times at the end of the second. Management said this rise reflects the $23 billion of EchoStar spectrum licenses bought at the end of July.

Is Tutor Perini (TPC) a Buy as Wall Street Analysts Look Optimistic?

Trading disclosure

Investors often turn to recommendations made by Wall Street analysts before making a Buy, Sell, or Hold decision about a stock. While media reports about rating changes by these brokerage-firm employed (or sell-side) analysts often affect a stock's price, do they really matter?

Let's take a look at what these Wall Street heavyweights have to say about Tutor Perini (TPC) before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage.

Tutor Perini currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.33, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by six brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.33 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy.

Of the six recommendations that derive the current ABR, five are Strong Buy, representing 83.3% of all recommendations.

Brokerage Recommendation Trends for TPC
Broker Rating Breakdown Chart for TPC

Check price target & stock forecast for Tutor Perini here>>>

The ABR suggests buying Tutor Perini, but making an investment decision solely on the basis of this information might not be a good idea. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation.

Do you wonder why? As a result of the vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover, their analysts tend to rate it with a strong positive bias. According to our research, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations for every "Strong Sell" recommendation.

In other words, their interests aren't always aligned with retail investors, rarely indicating where the price of a stock could actually be heading. Therefore, the best use of this information could be validating your own research or an indicator that has proven to be highly successful in predicting a stock's price movement.

With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, which classifies stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), is a reliable indicator of a stock's near-term price performance. So, validating the Zacks Rank with ABR could go a long way in making a profitable investment decision.

ABR Should Not Be Confused With Zacks Rank

In spite of the fact that Zacks Rank and ABR both appear on a scale from 1 to 5, they are two completely different measures.

The ABR is calculated solely based on brokerage recommendations and is typically displayed with decimals (example: 1.28). In contrast, the Zacks Rank is a quantitative model allowing investors to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.

Tutor Perini has been on a remarkable share price run in recent years, which puts fresh focus on whether that move lines up with the cash the business is expected to generate. With the stock now around three figures, the key issue for investors is how that price stacks up against an estimate of intrinsic value based on its cash flows.

Over the past 3 years the share price has delivered a very large gain that puts substantial expectations on the company to keep turning project wins into durable cash generation.

Recent contract awards and record reported results suggest a sizeable backlog and busy project pipeline, which can support visibility on future cash inflows and the timing of those flows.

If you'd rather focus on earnings, this one's for you. See what Tutor Perini's 37.8x P/E says about the price.

Is Tutor Perini a Bargain on Cash Flow?
